name: Kannada
description: Conversational Kannada for people who already speak one Indian language. Where the grammar carries over from Tamil or Malayalam, we say so and use it.

units.title: Foundations
units.description: Greetings, basic courtesies, yes and no. By the end of this unit you can survive your first day on the street.

lessons.title: Greetings
lessons.description: Five words. By the end you'll hold a real four-line greeting exchange.

vocabulary.notes: Neutral and respectful. Works in every register — to a stranger, an elder, a shopkeeper. The default greeting.

ta.note: Different word, same job. நமஸ்காரம் also exists in Tamil as a Sanskrit borrowing.

ml.note: Direct cognate — Kannada drops the final -m.

vocabulary.notes: Literally 'how-are-you-being'. The -īrā ending marks formal/plural respect. Use this with anyone older than you or anyone you've just met.

ta.note: Same structure: 'how' + 'are you' + respect marker. The -īṅga ending matches Kannada's -īrā.

ml.note: Same pattern. Malayalam compresses the respect marker into context rather than a suffix.

vocabulary.notes: Breaks into chennāgi (well) + iddēne (I am). The -ēne ending is first-person. You'll see this ending everywhere — remember it.

ta.note: Same architecture: adverb + 'I am'. nallā maps to chennāgi, irukkēn maps to iddēne. The -ēn / -ēne first-person ending is the same root.

ml.note: Different word for 'well' (sukha, Sanskrit-origin), but the -māṇ copula does the same work as iddēne.

vocabulary.notes: When you toss the question back. Pronounced like 'NEE-voo'. The informal singular is ನೀನು (nīnu) — use that only with friends and kids.

ta.note: Same root nī- with a respect suffix. Kannada uses -vu, Tamil uses -ṅga.

ml.note: Same nī- root. Malayalam preserves the older -ṅṅaḷ ending.

vocabulary.notes: Sanskrit-origin, used across South India. The -gaḷu ending is plural — literally 'thanks-plural', because one thanks isn't enough. In casual speech 'thanks' (in English) is just as common.

ta.note: Pure Tamil word, more common than the Sanskrit ధన்யவாதம். Both exist but nandri wins in speech.

ml.note: Same Dravidian root as Tamil nandri.

exercises.explanation: ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ is the default neutral greeting — works for anyone, any time of day.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 'How are you?' (formal)
exercises.explanation: The -īrā ending is the formal/plural respect marker. Use it with anyone you wouldn't call by their first name.
Breaks into chennāgi (well) + iddēne (I am). The -ēne ending = first person 'I'.
ನೀವು = you (formal). Tossing the question back is what closes the loop in any greeting exchange.
Sanskrit-origin. The -gaḷu ending makes it plural — Kannada speakers say 'thanks-plural' because once isn't enough.

exercises.prompt: Build: 'I'm well, thank you. And you?'
exercises.explanation: This is a complete return-turn in a greeting exchange. You can now hold all four lines: ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ → ಹೇಗಿದ್ದೀರಾ → ಚೆನ್ನಾಗಿದ್ದೇನೆ, ಧನ್ಯವಾದಗಳು. ನೀವು?

exercises.prompt: You meet your girlfriend's mother for the first time. She says ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ. What do you say back?
exercises.explanation: Mirror the greeting, then take the conversational initiative. Skipping ಹೇಗಿದ್ದೀರಾ feels cold — like a flat 'hi' in English.

bridges.ta: If you already speak Tamil, the structural moves here will feel familiar: respect suffixes (-īrā ↔ -īṅga), first-person endings (-ēne ↔ -ēn), and the nī- root for 'you'. The vocabulary differs but the grammar is the same shape.
bridges.ml: Malayalam speakers will spot the Sanskrit borrowings instantly (ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ, ಧನ್ಯವಾದ). The native Dravidian forms (ಚೆನ್ನಾಗಿ, ನೀವು) follow the same logic as Malayalam but with different suffixes.
